options: Point of Contact
Proof of Concept
Plan of Completion
Process of Change
Product of Choice
questions.explanation: POC stands for Proof of Concept.

questions.stem: What is the goal of a POC?
options: To make sure whether an idea is feasible or not
To deliver the final production system
To train end users on the software
To choose the cheapest hardware
To complete user acceptance testing
questions.explanation: The goal of a POC is to make sure whether the idea is feasible or not.

questions.stem: In a POC, what is most important?
options: The technology used
The size of the infrastructure
The output
The number of developers
The licensing cost
questions.explanation: In a POC the output is most important, not the technology.

questions.stem: What context does a POC normally follow?
options: The security context of the network
The legal context of the contract
The maintenance context of the system
The sales context of the product
The archival context of the data
questions.explanation: A POC normally follows the sales context of the product.

questions.stem: For whom is a POC built and run?
options: Database administrators
Technical developers
External auditors
Regulators
Business users
questions.explanation: A POC is built and run for business users.

questions.stem: What do implementers make sure of during a POC?
options: That the output fulfils customer requirements and convinces the business that this is the solution to go with
That the production infrastructure is fully sized
That all unit tests pass
That the data model is normalised
That the solution complies with external audit standards
questions.explanation: In a POC the implementers make sure the output fulfils customer requirements and convince the business that this is the solution to go with.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a POC?
options: It tests whether an idea is feasible
It is built for business users
It prioritises the technology over the output
It follows the sales context of a product
It aims to convince the business of the solution
questions.explanation: A POC prioritises the output, not the technology; the other statements describe a POC correctly.

questions.stem: Which question does a POC set out to answer?
options: How much will the production licences cost?
Is the idea feasible?
Which developers should be hired?
How will the final user interface look?
Which SCD type should be used?
questions.explanation: A POC exists to make sure whether the idea is feasible or not.

questions.stem: Whom must a POC convince that the proposed approach is the solution to go with?
options: The hardware vendor
The internal audit team
The network administrators
The business
The external regulator
questions.explanation: During a POC the implementers convince the business that this is the solution to go with.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarises a POC?
options: A full-scale production deployment with complete data
A technical evaluation using dummy data for developers
A small release of real features to actual users
A formal test of system integration
A feasibility check whose output must satisfy customer requirements and win over the business
questions.explanation: A POC checks whether the idea is feasible, with the output fulfilling customer requirements and convincing the business; it is built and run for business users.
